extracted.intended_audience: general public; readers of entertainment/news about comedians and public controversies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit norms about boundaries in stand-up comedy, how comedians should respond when material offends, and how audience/social reaction can escalate controversies. Focused on public apologies and remediation after offensive material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hateful or bullying remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedic material should not bully or make people feel bad about who they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from Morgan: "I don't have a hateful bone in my body," and "I don't believe that anyone should be bullied or just made to feel bad about who they are." The article frames anti-gay statements (e.g., threats of violence) as unacceptable and offensive to audience members and advocacy groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize when material is beyond acceptable comedic context
rubrics_metrics.description: Some comments are "not funny in any context."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes Morgan's earlier statement that his comments were "not funny in any context," signalling a standard that certain expressions (especially that advocate violence or target identities) are categorically inappropriate regardless of intent or persona.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge when a performer "went too far"
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians with an outrageous persona must nonetheless admit responsibility when material crosses a line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece says Morgan is "known for an outrageous, unpredictable comedy style where few subjects are taboo," but also that "even Morgan admits he went too far," indicating an expectation that performers self-assess and concede when material is harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial actions: personal apology and direct engagement with affected groups
rubrics_metrics.description: When material offends, make a personal apology and meet with offended individuals/groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morgan returned to Nashville to deliver a personal apology to gay advocacy groups and audience members, met with gay rights advocates and some attendees, and earlier met with homeless lesbian and gay youth in New York. He spoke with the offended audience member(s) before addressing reporters. These actions are presented as appropriate remediation steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid defensive public Q&A when issuing apology
rubrics_metrics.description: Apologies may be delivered without taking questions from the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes Morgan met with advocates and "did not take questions" when addressing reporters, suggesting a model where apologies are given directly to affected parties and not used as media soundbites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and social media can amplify offense and prompt accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience reactions, especially when shared on social media, can escalate a comedian's remarks into a wider controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites an audience member, Kevin Rogers, whose Facebook post brought widespread attention to the routine, illustrating how online sharing can drive public response and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance comedic freedom with public responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A comedian's history of tackling taboo subjects does not exempt them from consequences when speech harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the article acknowledges Morgan's history of addressing homosexual themes with little outcry, it underscores that ongoing reputation for edgy material does not negate responsibility to refrain from violent or demeaning statements.
